title: You’re Not Born Confident. You Prepare for It. | Jim Keyes
guest: Jim Keyes, former CEO of 7-Eleven and Blockbuster, author of Education Is Freedom
summary: A director's-cut replay of the hosts' conversation with Jim Keyes, who went from a three-room house with no plumbing to running two Fortune 500 companies, followed by the sisters' takeaways months later. Keyes lays out his three Cs (change equals opportunity, confidence is learned by preparing to win, clarity through simplicity), argues education is freedom, and rewrites the Blockbuster story as a cash-management failure rather than a technology one; the hosts take away agency, lifelong curiosity, and the power of clear communication.

ideas.idea: Change equals opportunity: you cannot control what happens in the environment, but you have full agency over how you respond to it.
ideas.detail: Keyes notes the acronym CEO in 'change equals opportunity' and says all commerce begins and ends with something changing. He took the Blockbuster CEO job to move it to digital streaming, could not predict the Lehman Brothers collapse, and had to pivot from transforming the company to saving it through restructuring and a sale to Dish Network. He could not change being born into a screwed-up situation, but chose not to be its victim.

ideas.idea: Confidence is not something you are born with; it is learned, and the formula is three words: prepare to win.
ideas.detail: Keyes got the phrase from author Harvey Mackay (Swim with the Sharks Without Being Eaten Alive) while writing his confidence chapter. Tom Brady walks onto the field confident because he studied game tape, and a pilot stays calm in turbulence because of simulation time; the more prepared you are, the more confident you can be and the better your chance of winning.
names_or_cases: Swim with the Sharks Without Being Eaten Alive

ideas.idea: Preparation is not tricking your brain but using neuroplasticity to genuinely reprogram it with new patterns, including in relationships.
ideas.detail: The brain runs on preset patterns, some with fear built in, and can be rewired. Applied to love, this means learning to respond with your own agency rather than reverting to the same bad patterns and being pushed into reactions by your partner.

ideas.idea: Clarity means simplicity: break things down into simple terms through inbound clarity (listening effectively) and outbound clarity (communicating simply).
ideas.detail: Keyes cites Da Vinci and Coco Chanel on elegance in simplicity and says we over-complicate everything in a world of information. Cherie reframes clarity as a force field protecting your goals from negative inputs.

ideas.idea: The three Cs work together: embrace change, have the confidence to act on it, and the clarity to execute; together they eliminate fear.
ideas.detail: Without clarity and listening you will not see change coming and will not have confidence, so any one alone is insufficient. The hosts note that distilling his philosophy into three Cs is itself a masterclass in communication.

ideas.idea: Relentless (not toxic) positivity is a good way to live because it keeps you focused on what you want to do, but faked positivity is toxic because it is not genuine.
ideas.detail: Cherie says the world is already negative enough, so controlling your own positivity keeps you on track; Keyes agrees but distinguishes genuine positivity that comes from blocking out noise from faked positivity.

ideas.idea: Education is freedom: material things can be taken from you, but knowledge cannot, and it buys freedom of time, choice and exploring the world.
ideas.detail: Keyes's father never made it past sixth grade and was tied to his factory machine; when young Jim offered to work to put plumbing in the house, his father said no, learning was his number one job. The hosts' catchphrase 'information is power' is a variant: without information you cannot make informed decisions, and they see education as the tool for socioeconomic mobility in America.

ideas.idea: Cultural literacy is a career superpower: learning even a little of another language reveals differences that Americans otherwise misread as integrity issues.
ideas.detail: Keyes learned 'taxi cab Japanese' while steering 7-Eleven through Japanese ownership. In Japanese, 'hai' means 'I acknowledge you,' not 'I agree,' so Americans who think a contract point was agreed are shocked to renegotiate it the next day. He also studied abroad in the UK in college.

ideas.idea: Americans are becoming lazier, not dumber: easy access to information lets perception replace perspective and critical thinking.
ideas.detail: Perception is taking something at face value; critical thinking, which separates humans from other species, is needed to determine truth rather than accepting what you read or saw on the news.

ideas.idea: Blockbuster did not die from missing technology; it died from cash management, and the Harvard case study gets the lesson wrong.
ideas.detail: Blockbuster had a billion dollars of debt coming due in 2009 when banks were shut during the 2008 crisis. In 2000 it partnered with Enron on streaming bandwidth, and in 2007 Keyes's first move was buying MovieLink, a streaming company built by five of the six major studios. He says the case belongs in the accounting or change-management course: for any entrepreneur, cash flow is oxygen.

ideas.idea: Keyes's biggest regret at Blockbuster was letting Carl Icahn talk him into joining as public-company CEO instead of taking it private with private equity.
ideas.topic: Finance industry: VC, PE, banking, hedge funds
ideas.detail: His plan was to partner with PE, take Blockbuster private, do the digital transformation and re-emerge public five years later; Icahn argued 'I'm the financial guy, you're the operator.' Had he taken it private, 100% of the debt would have been refinanced to come due in 2012 and the company would have sailed through the financial crisis.

ideas.idea: 7-Eleven wins globally by localizing products through local licensees rather than running one menu like Starbucks or KFC.
ideas.detail: Japan has onigiri, Taiwan tea eggs, Korea kimbap, Sweden in-store baked breads. Keyes pitched an Americanized onigiri and a barbecue-and-coleslaw bento to his largely Japanese board, who looked at him like an idiot, but he still believes Americanizing onigiri is an opportunity, as pizza and Taco Bell tacos were Americanized.

ideas.idea: Regulation and cold-chain management, not lack of will, explain why Japanese-quality convenience food does not exist in US 7-Elevens, and the fix is working with authorities to modernize standards.
ideas.detail: US food-safety law restricts the butter content that makes Japanese bread soft, and US refrigeration must be kept around 35-40 degrees versus much warmer chilled temperatures in Japan, which dries out bread. Because temperature can now be measured electronically with immediate dispatch, companies could petition for slightly higher thresholds and better product.

ideas.idea: China's opening was a once-in-history business moment: the Beijing government flew to Dallas to ask 7-Eleven for 500 stores in time for the 2008 Olympics and delivered.
ideas.detail: 7-Eleven already had stores in Hong Kong and Guangdong but none in mainland China; the request came a year and a half before the Olympics and seemed impossible. Keyes recalls Beijing going from more bicycles than cars to Mercedes everywhere in five years.

ideas.idea: To stay ahead of the curve as you age, engage your inner child, stay wide-eyed curious, and use creativity to defy the conservatism that creeps in with age.
ideas.detail: At 70, Keyes invests in space, advanced energy, AI and AR, and paints, sculpts and writes music despite never expecting to be good at them ('intelligence having fun'). Learning happens outside your comfort zone; there is no such thing as failure when trying something new. The hosts note he is even taking pilot lessons.

ideas.idea: You can decide not to let old-age conservatism creep in, and your life education never has to end.
ideas.detail: The hosts say Keyes has 'golden retriever energy' and the self-described maturity of a 12-year-old, doing brand-new things in his 70s, which makes them aspire to still be trying new things at 72.

ideas.idea: You are the captain of your own ship: analysis paralysis is a valid first response, but power and determination together can change your situation if you stick at it.
ideas.detail: Cherie's takeaway from Keyes's full-agency story is that the episode is a reminder of the different ways to get unstuck, and that change should make you less scared because amazing things come from it.

ideas.idea: Talking with great leaders teaches communication by osmosis: Keyes makes complex concepts feel simple and conversational without lecturing.
ideas.detail: Rewatching, the hosts realized the conversation was casually a business masterclass covering supply chain, cold-chain management, cash management and cross-cultural business, delivered with clarity and catchphrases like 'prepare to win' and 'change equals opportunity'.
